title: QMA versus QCMA
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QCMA}\) for ordinary promise problems without an oracle? Equivalently, does every promise problem that has a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with polynomially many quantum witness qubits also have such a verifier with only polynomially many classical witness bits, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\)? The converse inclusion is available by measuring a purported classical witness in the computational basis, so the requested equality is exactly the inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QCMA}\).
why: This asks whether an untrusted quantum state can certify something that no short classical message can certify, even when the recipient already has a quantum computer. It isolates the power of the evidence itself from the power of the verifier and is a basic boundary in quantum complexity.

progress.text: Aaronson–Kuperberg separate quantum and classical witnesses relative to a quantum oracle.
Bostanci–Haferkamp–Nirkhe–Zhandry post an unconditional separation relative to a standard classical oracle; the revised manuscript is dated 17 January 2026 and appears at STOC 2026.

Bostanci–Huang–Vaikuntanathan give a simpler classical-oracle proof using good codes; the checked ECCC revision is dated 12 April and also separates quantum from classical advice in that oracle setting.

context_blocks.text: Both sides allow quantum computation. A classical certificate may tell the verifier which quantum experiment to perform; it need not describe a quantum witness state. Consequently, showing that some state needs many classical bits to describe does not establish a separation of the verification classes.

Soundness is essential: a verifier must reject a no-instance for every permitted witness. A proof that works only when the prover follows the intended preparation is not a QMA or QCMA verification guarantee. The mathematical model makes this universal quantifier explicit.

Aaronson–Kuperberg gave a separation after both verifiers are granted access to the same quantum black box. This supplied evidence about black-box methods while leaving the ordinary classes without that extra resource unresolved.

The November 2025 manuscript, published at STOC 2026, strengthens the oracle type to a standard classical function. Classical here describes the function encoded by the oracle, not a requirement to ask only classical queries: the quantum verifiers can query it in superposition. The result remains relative to an oracle.

The 2026 good-code construction gives a simpler classical-oracle separation and extends to quantum versus classical advice. Advice is trusted information that depends only on input length; a witness is untrusted information tailored to the individual input. The advice theorem is therefore recorded as related work, not as a replacement of this card’s witness question.

An ordinary separation would require an explicit promise problem and a lower bound against every uniform classical-witness quantum verifier. The checked oracle theorems do not remove their black box, so they do not justify marking the original class comparison resolved.

answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{QMA}\subseteq\mathrm{QCMA}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation: there exists a disjoint promise pair in QMA for which no uniform polynomial-time QCMA verifier meets both guarantees. The affirmative direction must cover every QMA promise problem, with a possibly different verifier and polynomial witness bound. A negative proof must quantify over all eligible classical-witness verifiers. An oracle separation, a gap between two particular verifiers, or a quantum state's large classical description length does not alone settle the target. The output is a proof of class equality or strict containment, not an approximation to an acceptance probability.
definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

The class \(\mathrm{QCMA}\), quantum classical Merlin–Arthur, uses the same uniform quantum verifier model, but its witness is a binary string \(w\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), loaded in the computational-basis state \(|w\rangle\). For every yes-input some such string must be accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every no-input every such string must be accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). Lengths can be padded to a polynomial bound. Classical witnesses are untrusted and may depend on the individual input. They are not trusted advice shared by all inputs of a given length. A QCMA verifier may perform general quantum computation after receiving the classical witness. Equality means equality of the sets of promise problems under these definitions, not equality of the two witness representations for a particular circuit.

importance.reason: Separates quantum from classical witnesses and therefore addresses a basic source of quantum computational power.

sentences: QMA and QCMA use efficient quantum verifiers but allow quantum and classical witnesses respectively.
A witness can depend on the entire input and is untrusted, so soundness must hold against every permitted message.
The question is equality of the ordinary uniform promise classes without oracle access or shared advice.
Quantum-oracle and, more recently, classical-oracle separations give evidence about the role of quantum witnesses without separating the ordinary classes.
The revised card fixes the finite-circuit model and requires a complete Lean proof of containment or a universally valid separating problem.
